topics.title: Scalars
topics.summary: A scalar is a single real number — magnitude with no direction.
topics.intuition: Temperature, mass, speed: a lone number. Contrast with a vector which also carries direction.

steps.text: A scalar c ∈ ℝ is just a real number.
Scalars can scale (stretch/shrink) vectors and matrices.

python.note: a plain Python float is a scalar

mistakes: Confusing scalar 0 with the zero vector
topics.example: Temperature 98.6°F is a scalar; wind velocity (speed + direction) is a vector.

walkthrough.problem: Scale the vector v = (2, −1, 3) by the scalar c = 3.

steps.note: Scalar multiplication multiplies every component by c.
Simplify each entry.

topics.title: Vectors
topics.summary: An ordered list of numbers representing magnitude and direction in n-dimensional space.
topics.intuition: An arrow in space: where it points and how long it is. Adding two vectors tip-to-tail gives a new vector.

steps.text: A vector v ∈ ℝⁿ is an ordered n-tuple of real numbers.
Vectors support addition (component-wise) and scalar multiplication.
The zero vector 0 is the additive identity.

python.note: NumPy is the standard for LA in Python

mistakes: Row vs column vector confusion — always use column vectors (n×1) by convention
topics.example: Velocity in 3-D space: v = [3, -1, 2] means 3 m/s east, 1 m/s south, 2 m/s up.

walkthrough.problem: Add v = (3, −1, 2) and w = (1, 4, −1), and compute 2v.

steps.note: Vector addition is component-wise.
Scalar multiplication scales every component.

topics.title: Vector Operations
topics.summary: Addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, and magnitude — the building blocks of all linear algebra.
topics.intuition: Vectors obey 8 axioms that define a vector space. Every operation we do on matrices ultimately reduces to vector operations.

steps.text: Addition: (u + v)ᵢ = uᵢ + vᵢ
Scalar multiplication: (cv)ᵢ = c·vᵢ
Magnitude: ‖v‖ = √(v₁² + … + vₙ²)
Unit vector: v̂ = v / ‖v‖

python.note: unit vector pointing same direction as v

mistakes: Forgetting to normalize before using as a direction
topics.example: Wind direction: normalize velocity vector to get a pure direction.

walkthrough.problem: For u = (1, 2) and v = (3, −1), find u − v, ‖v‖, and the unit vector in the direction of v.

steps.note: Subtraction is component-wise.
Magnitude is the square root of the sum of squared components.
The unit vector divides v by its own magnitude.

topics.title: Dot Product
topics.summary: Dot product u·v = Σ uᵢvᵢ = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ — measures how aligned two vectors are.
topics.intuition: If u·v = 0 the vectors are perpendicular. If positive they point the same general direction. This is the engine behind projections, angles, and orthogonality.

steps.text: Algebraic definition: u·v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂ + … + uₙvₙ
Geometric definition: u·v = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ
Dot product is symmetric: u·v = v·u
Orthogonality condition: u·v = 0 ⟺ u ⊥ v

python.note: cosine of angle between u and v

mistakes: Using dot product on vectors of different dimensions
topics.example: Work done by force F over displacement d: W = F·d

walkthrough.problem: Two vectors get reused through this whole chain: v₁ = (1, 1, 0) and v₂ = (1, 0, 1). Compute v₁·v₂ and v₁·v₁ — both feed straight into Projection below.

topics.title: Cross Product
topics.summary: Cross product u × v produces a vector perpendicular to both u and v (only in ℝ³).
topics.intuition: The magnitude ‖u × v‖ = ‖u‖‖v‖sin θ equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by u and v. Direction follows the right-hand rule.

steps.text: Only defined in ℝ³.
u × v = (u₂v₃−u₃v₂, u₃v₁−u₁v₃, u₁v₂−u₂v₁)
Anti-commutative: u × v = −(v × u)
‖u × v‖ = area of parallelogram spanned by u and v

mistakes: Applying cross product to vectors in ℝ² or ℝⁿ for n≠3
topics.example: Torque τ = r × F — the rotational effect of force F at position r.

walkthrough.problem: Compute u × v for the standard basis vectors u = (1,0,0) and v = (0,1,0).

steps.note: Set up the symbolic determinant formula for the cross product.
Expand along the top row using 2×2 cofactors.
Each 2×2 determinant evaluates directly.
The magnitude of u × v equals the area of the parallelogram (here, the unit square) spanned by u and v.

topics.title: Matrices
topics.summary: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. An m×n matrix has m rows and n columns.
topics.intuition: Think of a matrix as a compact encoding of a linear transformation — it takes vectors in and gives vectors out.

steps.text: An m×n matrix A has entries Aᵢⱼ (row i, column j).
The columns of A are vectors in ℝᵐ; the rows are vectors in ℝⁿ.
Square matrix: m = n. Rectangular: m ≠ n.

mistakes: 1-indexed in MATLAB vs 0-indexed in Python/NumPy
topics.example: A 3×3 rotation matrix rotates every vector in ℝ³ by a fixed angle.

walkthrough.problem: For A = [[2,1],[1,3]], identify the entries Aᵢⱼ and the matrix's shape.

steps.note: Aᵢⱼ denotes the entry in row i, column j.
Count rows and columns to get the shape.
steps.latex: A \text{ has } 2 \text{ rows and } 2 \text{ columns} \;\Longrightarrow\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}

topics.title: Matrix Operations
topics.summary: Addition, scalar multiplication, transpose, and matrix multiplication.
topics.intuition: Matrix multiplication AB means 'apply transformation B, then A'. Order matters — AB ≠ BA in general.

steps.text: Addition: (A+B)ᵢⱼ = Aᵢⱼ + Bᵢⱼ — same dimensions required.
Transpose: (Aᵀ)ᵢⱼ = Aⱼᵢ — rows become columns.
Matrix-vector product Av: the i-th entry is the dot product of row i with v.
Matrix multiplication AB: (AB)ᵢⱼ = row i of A · column j of B. A must be m×k, B must be k×n.

python.note: WARNING: this is element-wise, not matrix multiply

matlab.note: matrix multiply — * is matrix multiply by default

mistakes: Using * in Python for matrix multiplication (it's element-wise); use @
topics.example: Applying two transformations in sequence: rotate then scale = S·R applied to vector v.

walkthrough.problem: For A = [[2,1],[1,3]] and B = [[1,0],[2,1]], compute A+B, A·B, and Bᵗ.

steps.note: Addition is entry-wise.
Each entry of A·B is a dot product of a row of A with a column of B.
Transpose swaps rows and columns: entry (i,j) moves to (j,i). A is symmetric so its transpose wouldn't visibly change — use B instead, which isn't symmetric, so the swap is actually visible.
Check entry-by-entry: B's (2,1) entry was 2 — it moved to position (1,2) in Bᵗ. B's (1,2) entry was 0 — it moved to position (2,1).

topics.title: Determinant
topics.summary: det(A) is a scalar that measures volume scaling and tells you if A is invertible.
topics.intuition: The determinant is the signed area (2-D) or volume (3-D) of the parallelogram/parallelepiped formed by the column vectors. If det = 0, the columns are linearly dependent and the matrix is singular.

steps.text: Larger matrices: cofactor expansion along any row or column.
det(AB) = det(A)·det(B)
det(Aᵀ) = det(A)
A is invertible ⟺ det(A) ≠ 0

mistakes: det = 0 means NO inverse, not that something went wrong numerically
topics.example: A 2×2 shear matrix has det = 1 — it preserves area but skews shapes.

walkthrough.problem: Compute det(A) for A = [[2,1],[1,3]] via cofactor expansion.

steps.note: Cofactor expansion along the first row: det(A) = a·C₁₁ − b·C₁₂, where for a 2×2 matrix the cofactors are just the opposite diagonal entries.
Simplify.

topics.title: Systems of Linear Equations
topics.summary: A system Ax = b: find vectors x satisfying all equations simultaneously.
topics.intuition: Each equation is a hyperplane. The solution is where all hyperplanes intersect — could be a point, a line, a plane, or nothing.

steps.text: Write the system as an augmented matrix [A | b].
Apply row reduction to find solutions.
Three cases: unique solution, infinitely many, no solution.

matlab.note: backslash = solve — most important MATLAB operator

mistakes: Using inv(A)*b instead of A\b in MATLAB — slower and less numerically stable
topics.example: 3 unknown currents in a circuit → 3 equations → solve the 3×3 system.

steps.note: Write the augmented matrix [A | b].
Swap rows so the pivot is 1 (or scale row 1 by 1/2) — swap R1 and R2 for a clean pivot.
Eliminate the entry below the pivot: R2 → R2 − 2R1.
Solve the second row for y, then back-substitute into the first row.
Verify in the original equations.

topics.title: Row Reduction & RREF
topics.summary: Reduced Row Echelon Form: a systematic algorithm to solve systems, find rank, null space, and inverses.
topics.intuition: Row operations don't change solutions — they just simplify the equations until the answer is obvious. RREF is the simplest possible form.

steps.text: Three legal row operations: swap, scale, add multiple of one row to another.
REF: each pivot is to the right of the one above; zeros below pivots.
RREF: additionally, each pivot = 1 and zeros ABOVE pivots too.
Pivot columns correspond to basic variables; free columns = free variables.

python.note: SymPy for exact RREF (NumPy gives numerical)

mistakes: Forgetting to back-substitute: RREF gives you the answer directly, no extra step
topics.example: Solving a 3-variable system: augment [A|b], row-reduce, read off x from RREF.

walkthrough.problem: Row-reduce A to its Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF).

steps.note: Eliminate below the first pivot (column 1): R2 ← R2 − 2R1.
Continue eliminating column 1: R3 ← R3 − R1.
Row 2 is all zeros and row 3 has the next pivot, so swap them: R2 ↔ R3.
Scale row 2 so the pivot in column 2 equals 1: R2 ← −R2.
Clear above the column-2 pivot: R1 ← R1 − 2R2. This gives the RREF.
Pivots sit in columns 1 and 2 (column 3 is free) — this matrix has rank 2.

topics.title: Matrix Inverse
topics.summary: A⁻¹ is the unique matrix such that AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. Only square, full-rank matrices have inverses.
topics.intuition: The inverse undoes the transformation A. If A rotates 30°, A⁻¹ rotates −30°. If det(A) = 0, the transformation is irreversible (collapses a dimension).

steps.text: A is invertible ⟺ det(A) ≠ 0 ⟺ A has full rank.
Compute A⁻¹ via augmented form [A | I] → RREF → [I | A⁻¹].
2×2 shortcut: if A = [[a,b],[c,d]], A⁻¹ = (1/det) [[d,-b],[-c,a]]
(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹

python.note: should be identity (up to float error)

mistakes: Never use inv(A)*b to solve Ax=b — always use A\b or np.linalg.solve
topics.example: Decoding a linear cipher: apply the inverse of the encoding matrix to get plain text.

walkthrough.problem: Find the inverse of B using the adjugate (cofactor) method.

steps.note: First confirm B is invertible by checking its determinant.
Compute the four cofactors. Each cofactor deletes the row/column of that entry, takes the determinant of what's left, and applies a sign (−1)^{i+j}.
The adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
Divide the adjugate by the determinant.
Verify B B⁻¹ = I.

topics.title: Rank & Nullity
topics.summary: Rank = number of pivot columns = dimension of the column space. Rank + Nullity = n (number of columns).
topics.intuition: Rank tells you how many independent directions A can reach. Nullity tells you how many directions A collapses to zero. Together they always sum to n.

steps.text: Apply RREF to A. Count pivot columns → that's the rank.
Nullity = n − rank (the Rank-Nullity Theorem).
rank(A) = rank(Aᵀ): row rank equals column rank.

mistakes: Rank is a property of the matrix, not of individual rows or columns
topics.example: A 4×6 matrix can have rank at most 4. If rank = 3, nullity = 3.

walkthrough.problem: Verify the Rank-Nullity Theorem for A: rank(A) + nullity(A) = number of columns.

steps.note: Row-reduce A. The number of pivot columns is the rank.
Column 3 has no pivot, so it's free — that single free variable is the nullity.
A has n = 3 columns. Add rank and nullity together.

topics.title: Null Space (Kernel)
topics.summary: Null space of A = all vectors x such that Ax = 0. It's a subspace of ℝⁿ.
topics.intuition: The null space is what A 'kills' — directions that become zero. Its dimension (nullity) counts how many free variables you have in Ax = 0.

steps.text: Set up the homogeneous system Ax = 0 and row-reduce.
Free variables give parameters; express pivot variables in terms of free variables.
Write the general solution as a linear combination of basis vectors — that's the null space basis.

python.note: list of basis vectors for null space

matlab.note: columns of N span the null space

mistakes: Null space is only for Ax=0; for Ax=b solutions, add a particular solution to the null space
topics.example: The null space of a 3-D rotation matrix is just {0} — rotations are invertible.

walkthrough.problem: Find a basis for the null space of A by solving Ax = 0.

steps.note: Row-reduce the augmented system [A | 0] — the right-hand side stays 0 throughout.
Read off the equations. Columns 1 and 2 are pivot columns (x₁, x₂ basic); column 3 is free.
steps.latex: \begin{cases} x_1 + x_3 = 0 \\ x_2 + x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \;\Longrightarrow\; x_1 = -x_3, \quad x_2 = -x_3, \quad x_3 \text{ free}

steps.note: Let x₃ = t and write the general solution as a scalar multiple of one vector.
steps.latex: x = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = t\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}

steps.note: Verify: plug the spanning vector back into A.

topics.title: Column Space (Range)
topics.summary: Column space of A = span of the columns of A = all possible outputs Ax.
topics.intuition: The column space is every vector b that Ax = b can possibly reach. The system Ax = b is consistent iff b is in the column space.

steps.text: Row-reduce A. The pivot columns of the ORIGINAL A are a basis for col(A).
dim(col(A)) = rank(A).
Ax = b is solvable iff b ∈ col(A), i.e., rank([A|b]) = rank(A).

python.note: list of basis vectors for column space

mistakes: Use original A's pivot columns as the basis, not the RREF pivot columns
topics.example: A camera projection matrix's column space is the set of all images that can be formed.

walkthrough.problem: Find a basis for the column space of A.

steps.note: Row-reduce A to identify the pivot columns.
Column 3 of the RREF is a combination of columns 1 and 2 (col₃ = col₁ + col₂), confirming it adds nothing new. Take the CORRESPONDING columns from the original A — not from the RREF.

These two columns are independent (neither is a scalar multiple of the other, since the last entries 1 and 1 force any multiple to be c=1, but the first entries 1 and 2 then disagree) and dim(Col(A)) = rank(A) = 2, so they form a basis.

topics.title: Linear Independence
topics.summary: Vectors v₁,…,vₖ are linearly independent if c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ=0 implies all cᵢ=0.
topics.intuition: No vector in the set is redundant — none can be written as a combination of the others. Dependence means there's overlap or redundancy.

steps.text: Form matrix A with the vectors as columns.
Solve Ac = 0. If only c=0 works, the vectors are independent.
Equivalently: rank(A) = k (number of vectors) iff independent.

mistakes: Don't confuse independence of vectors with invertibility of the matrix (only applies when square)
topics.example: Standard basis vectors e₁, e₂, e₃ in ℝ³ are the canonical example of independence.

walkthrough.problem: Are the columns of A linearly independent? Test by solving c₁a₁ + c₂a₂ + c₃a₃ = 0.
walkthrough.problemLatex: a_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad a_2=\begin{bmatrix}2\\4\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad a_3=\begin{bmatrix}3\\6\\2\end{bmatrix}, \qquad c_1 a_1 + c_2 a_2 + c_3 a_3 = 0

steps.note: Stack the vectors as columns of A and solve Ac = 0 — this is exactly the null space computation.
We already found the null space is 1-dimensional, not just {0} — so a nonzero solution exists.
Take t = 1 as an explicit nontrivial dependence: −a₁ − a₂ + a₃ = 0, i.e. a₃ = a₁ + a₂.

Since a nontrivial solution (c≠0) exists, {a₁,a₂,a₃} is linearly DEPENDENT. Contrast: {a₁,a₂} alone has only the trivial solution (its matrix has rank 2 = number of vectors), so {a₁,a₂} IS independent — this is exactly the basis found for Col(A).

walkthrough.answerLatex: \{a_1,a_2,a_3\} \text{ is linearly dependent } (a_3 = a_1+a_2); \quad \{a_1,a_2\} \text{ is linearly independent}

topics.title: Basis & Coordinates
topics.summary: A basis is a linearly independent spanning set. Coordinates express any vector as a unique linear combination of basis vectors.
topics.intuition: A basis is a measuring system. Changing bases is like switching from miles to kilometers — same reality, different numbers.

steps.text: A basis B = {v₁,…,vₙ} for a subspace S satisfies: (1) independent, (2) spans S.
Every subspace has infinitely many bases but they all have the same size (dimension).
Coordinate vector [x]_B: solve Bc = x to get coordinates c.
Standard basis for ℝⁿ: {e₁,…,eₙ}

python.note: vector to express in this basis
coordinates of x in basis B

mistakes: A basis must be linearly independent AND span the space — both conditions required
topics.example: Fourier basis: any periodic signal is a unique sum of sin/cos waves.

walkthrough.problem: Construct a basis for Col(A) and verify it satisfies both basis requirements.

steps.note: A basis needs two properties: (1) spans the space, (2) linearly independent. The pivot columns of A, a₁ and a₂, were already shown to be independent.
They also span Col(A), since every column of A — including the dependent a₃ — is a combination of a₁ and a₂.
Both conditions hold, so {a₁, a₂} is a basis for Col(A), and its size gives the dimension.
As a check, express a₃ in coordinates relative to this basis: solve a₃ = c₁a₁ + c₂a₂.

topics.title: Eigenvalues
topics.summary: λ is an eigenvalue of A if det(A − λI) = 0. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial.
topics.intuition: An eigenvalue is a scalar stretching factor. If Av = λv, then A doesn't rotate v — it just scales it by λ.

steps.text: Form the characteristic polynomial p(λ) = det(A − λI).
Solve p(λ) = 0. Each root is an eigenvalue.
Algebraic multiplicity: how many times λ appears as a root.
tr(A) = sum of eigenvalues; det(A) = product of eigenvalues.

matlab.note: D = diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, V = eigenvectors

mistakes: Complex eigenvalues are normal — they just mean rotation is involved
topics.example: PageRank: the dominant eigenvalue/vector of the web link matrix determines page importance.

walkthrough.problem: Find the eigenvalues of A.

steps.note: The third row/column only touch the diagonal entry 2, so the top-left 2×2 block B decouples completely from it — one eigenvalue is just that 2.
Eigenvalues of B solve det(B − λI) = 0.
Expand the determinant.
Set it to zero and factor.

topics.title: Eigenvectors
topics.summary: v is an eigenvector for eigenvalue λ if Av = λv and v ≠ 0. Find them by solving (A−λI)v = 0.
topics.intuition: Eigenvectors are the 'special directions' that A doesn't rotate — only stretches. They reveal the natural axes of the transformation.

steps.text: For each eigenvalue λ, compute A − λI.
Find null space of (A−λI) — every non-zero vector in it is an eigenvector.
The eigenspace for λ = null space of (A−λI) = span of the eigenvectors for λ.
Geometric multiplicity = dim of eigenspace ≤ algebraic multiplicity.

mistakes: Eigenvectors are only defined up to scalar multiples — there's no unique eigenvector for a given eigenvalue
topics.example: PCA: eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the principal components (variance directions).

walkthrough.problem: Find the eigenspace for each eigenvalue found above.

steps.note: λ = 4: solve (A − 4I)x = 0.
λ = 0: solve Ax = 0.
λ = 2: solve (A − 2I)x = 0.

topics.title: Diagonalization
topics.summary: A = PDP⁻¹ where D is diagonal (eigenvalues) and P has eigenvectors as columns.
topics.intuition: Diagonalization finds a basis where A acts as pure scaling. In that basis, Aᵏ is trivial — just raise each eigenvalue to the k-th power.

steps.text: Find all eigenvalues λ₁,…,λₙ.
Find corresponding eigenvectors v₁,…,vₙ. For A to be diagonalizable, you need n linearly independent eigenvectors.
Build P = [v₁|v₂|…|vₙ] and D = diag(λ₁,…,λₙ).
Then A = PDP⁻¹, so Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹.

matlab.note: P columns = eigenvectors, D = diagonal eigenvalues

mistakes: Not all matrices are diagonalizable — repeated eigenvalues with deficient eigenspaces cause failure
topics.example: Fibonacci sequence: the 2×2 Fibonacci matrix diagonalizes to give the closed-form formula.

walkthrough.problem: Diagonalize A using the eigenvalues {0, 4, 2} and eigenvectors found above.

steps.note: Put each eigenvector as a column of P, in the same order you’ll list the eigenvalues.
Put the matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of D, in that same column order.
Each column satisfies Av_i = \lambda_i v_i, so AP = PD. Multiply both sides by P⁻¹ — which means we actually need to compute it, not just write the symbol.
P has the same block structure as A: row/column 3 is just (0,0,1), so P⁻¹ comes from inverting the top-left 2×2 block B and leaving the trailing 1 alone. Start with det(B), exactly as in Determinant.
Invert B with the same adjugate formula as Matrix Inverse: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by det(B).
Verify with one entry of PP⁻¹ — row 1 of P dotted with column 1 of P⁻¹ should give 1.

topics.title: Inner Product
topics.summary: A generalization of the dot product — any operation ⟨u,v⟩ satisfying linearity, symmetry, and positive-definiteness.
topics.intuition: An inner product gives geometry to a vector space: angles, lengths, and orthogonality. The dot product is the most common inner product in ℝⁿ.

steps.text: Standard inner product in ℝⁿ: ⟨u,v⟩ = uᵀv = Σ uᵢvᵢ
Positive-definiteness: ⟨v,v⟩ > 0 for v ≠ 0
Induced norm: ‖v‖ = √⟨v,v⟩
Cauchy-Schwarz: |⟨u,v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖·‖v‖

mistakes: For complex vectors, inner product is conjugate-linear in the first argument: ⟨u,v⟩ = ū·v
topics.example: Signal processing: ⟨f,g⟩ = ∫f(t)g(t)dt is the L² inner product for functions.

walkthrough.problem: Confirm the standard dot product on v₁ = (1,1,0) and v₂ = (1,0,1) satisfies the inner-product axioms of symmetry and positive-definiteness.

steps.note: From the Dot Product walkthrough, ⟨v₁,v₂⟩ = v₁·v₂ = 1.
Symmetry axiom: swapping the order must give the same value.
Positive-definiteness axiom: ⟨v,v⟩ > 0 for any nonzero v. Test it on v₁.
Both axioms hold for these concrete vectors under the standard dot product.

topics.title: Orthogonality
topics.summary: Vectors u and v are orthogonal if ⟨u,v⟩ = 0. A set of mutually orthogonal unit vectors is orthonormal.
topics.intuition: Orthogonal = perpendicular in the generalized sense. Orthonormal bases are the easiest to work with — coordinates are just dot products.

steps.text: u ⊥ v iff ⟨u,v⟩ = 0
Orthonormal: mutually orthogonal AND each has unit length.
For an orthonormal set Q, coordinates are simple: cᵢ = ⟨x, qᵢ⟩
Pythagoras in any inner product space: ‖u+v‖² = ‖u‖² + ‖v‖² when u ⊥ v

mistakes: Orthogonal ≠ orthonormal; orthonormal also requires unit length
topics.example: i, j, k (the standard basis) are orthonormal. They're perpendicular and each has length 1.

walkthrough.problem: Are v₁ = (1, 1, 0) and v₂ = (1, 0, 1) orthogonal?

steps.text: Compute v₁·v₂ — already done in Dot Product: it equals 1.
Since v₁·v₂ = 1 ≠ 0, the vectors are NOT orthogonal. That gap is exactly what Gram-Schmidt below fixes.

topics.title: Projection
topics.summary: The projection of b onto subspace W is the closest point in W to b. Defined as proj_W(b) = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb.
topics.intuition: Drop a perpendicular from b to the subspace. Where it lands is the projection. The error vector (b − proj) is always perpendicular to the subspace.

steps.text: Project b onto a single vector a: proj_a(b) = (aᵀb / aᵀa) · a
Project onto a subspace spanned by columns of A: proj = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb
Projection matrix P = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ; it satisfies P² = P (idempotent) and Pᵀ = P.
If A has orthonormal columns Q, then P = QQᵀ (much simpler).

python.note: projection of b onto line spanned by a

mistakes: The projection is onto the subspace, not onto a vector — a vector spans a 1-D subspace
topics.example: Least-squares fitting: project b onto the column space of A to find the best-fit solution.

walkthrough.problem: Find the projection of v₂ = (1, 0, 1) onto v₁ = (1, 1, 0).

steps.text: proj_{v₁}(v₂) = (v₂·v₁ / v₁·v₁) v₁. From Dot Product: v₂·v₁ = 1 and v₁·v₁ = 2.
Scalar coefficient = 1/2.
Multiply the scalar by v₁: (1/2)(1, 1, 0) = (0.5, 0.5, 0).

topics.title: Gram-Schmidt Process
topics.summary: Converts any linearly independent set into an orthonormal basis for the same subspace.
topics.intuition: Take each vector, subtract off its projections onto all previous orthonormal vectors, then normalize. What remains is a new vector orthogonal to all previous ones.

steps.text: Start: q₁ = v₁/‖v₁‖
For k≥2: e_k = v_k − Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ⁻¹ ⟨v_k, qᵢ⟩qᵢ (subtract projections)
Normalize: q_k = e_k / ‖e_k‖
Result: {q₁,…,qₖ} is orthonormal with same span as {v₁,…,vₖ}.

matlab.note: QR decomposition gives orthonormal Q (= Gram-Schmidt output)
should be identity — Q is orthonormal

mistakes: Numerical Gram-Schmidt can lose orthogonality; use Modified Gram-Schmidt or QR in practice
topics.example: Orthonormal polynomial basis: Legendre polynomials are Gram-Schmidt applied to {1, x, x², …}.

walkthrough.problem: Orthogonalize v₁ = (1, 1, 0) and v₂ = (1, 0, 1).

steps.text: u₂ = v₂ − proj_{u₁}(v₂) = (1, 0, 1) − (0.5, 0.5, 0) = (0.5, −0.5, 1). The projection was computed above.

topics.title: QR Decomposition
topics.summary: A = QR where Q has orthonormal columns and R is upper triangular.
topics.intuition: QR is the numerically stable form of Gram-Schmidt. Q provides an orthonormal basis; R encodes how the original columns are expressed in that basis.

steps.text: Q columns are the Gram-Schmidt orthonormal vectors.
R is upper triangular: Rᵢⱼ = ⟨qᵢ, vⱼ⟩ for i≤j
For square A: Aᵀb = Rᵀ(Qᵀb) — use QR to solve normal equations stably.
QR is used inside eigenvalue algorithms (QR iteration).

python.note: (3,3) and (3,2) for full; (3,2) and (2,2) for thin
thin QR — usually what you want

mistakes: Full vs thin QR: thin QR (same column count) is usually what you need for least squares
topics.example: Solving least squares Ax≈b: x = R⁻¹(Qᵀb) — more stable than normal equations.

walkthrough.problem: Find the QR factorization of A = [[1,1],[1,0],[0,1]] — a 3×2 matrix, not square — whose columns are v₁ = (1,1,0) and v₂ = (1,0,1).

steps.text: Run Gram-Schmidt on the columns of A to get q₁, q₂ — done in full above.
R is upper triangular by construction: r₁₁ = ‖u₁‖ = √2, r₁₂ = q₁·v₂ = 1/√2, r₂₂ = ‖u₂‖ = √1.5, and r₂₁ = 0 because q₂ ⊥ v₁.
Verify: Q R = A.

topics.title: LU Decomposition
topics.summary: A = LU (or PA = LU) where L is lower triangular and U is upper triangular.
topics.intuition: LU is Gaussian elimination stored as a matrix. Once computed, you can solve Ax = b for many different b vectors cheaply by forward/back substitution.

steps.text: Gaussian elimination produces U (upper triangular); the multipliers fill L (lower triangular).
P is a permutation matrix for row pivoting — always needed in practice.
Solve Ly = Pb (forward substitution), then Ux = y (back substitution).
Cost: O(n³) once, then O(n²) per new right-hand side.

matlab.note: PA = LU — note different argument order from scipy

mistakes: Without partial pivoting (P), LU can fail even for invertible matrices
topics.example: FEM solvers: factor the stiffness matrix once, then solve for hundreds of load vectors cheaply.

walkthrough.problem: Factor A into a lower-triangular L and upper-triangular U with A = LU, using no row swaps.

steps.note: The pivot is the (1,1) entry. The multiplier for row 2 is the entry below the pivot divided by the pivot.
Eliminate the entry below the pivot: replace row 2 with row 2 minus the multiplier times row 1.
What's left after elimination is U.
L stores the multiplier used to zero out each entry, with 1's on the diagonal.
Verify by multiplying L and U back together.

topics.title: Orthogonal Matrices
topics.summary: A square matrix Q is orthogonal if QᵀQ = QQᵀ = I, i.e., Q⁻¹ = Qᵀ.
topics.intuition: Orthogonal matrices are rigid rotations/reflections — they preserve lengths and angles. The columns (and rows) form an orthonormal basis.

steps.text: Equivalent conditions: columns orthonormal, rows orthonormal, Qᵀ = Q⁻¹.
|det(Q)| = 1: det = +1 for rotation, −1 for reflection.
‖Qv‖ = ‖v‖ for all v — lengths preserved.
Eigenvalues of a real orthogonal matrix have absolute value 1.

mistakes: Real orthogonal matrices are not the same as 'orthogonal vectors' — the term is overloaded
topics.example: 3-D rotation matrices (used in robotics and 3-D graphics) are all orthogonal.

walkthrough.problem: A is symmetric, so the eigenvectors from Diagonalization are already orthogonal — normalize them to build an orthogonal matrix Q.

steps.note: Check the length of each eigenvector.
Normalize each one (divide by its length).
Assemble Q from the normalized columns and verify Qᵗ Q = I.

topics.title: Symmetric Matrices
topics.summary: A matrix S is symmetric if S = Sᵀ. Symmetric matrices always have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
topics.intuition: Symmetric matrices are the most well-behaved — they always diagonalize with an orthonormal basis. Covariance matrices, Laplacians, and Hessians are all symmetric.

steps.text: S = Sᵀ iff Sᵢⱼ = Sⱼᵢ for all i,j.
Spectral Theorem: every symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues.
Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
S is always orthogonally diagonalizable: S = QΛQᵀ with Q orthogonal.

python.note: eigh is for symmetric — more stable than eig

matlab.note: for symmetric A, V is automatically orthogonal

mistakes: Use np.linalg.eigh (not eig) for symmetric matrices — it's more stable and guarantees real values
topics.example: Covariance matrix of data is always symmetric positive semi-definite.

walkthrough.problem: Confirm A is symmetric by checking A = Aᵗ entrywise.

steps.note: Transpose A by flipping across the main diagonal.
Compare entrywise: every off-diagonal pair matches.
Since A = Aᵗ, A is symmetric — this is exactly why its eigenvectors came out orthogonal for free.

topics.title: Spectral Theorem
topics.summary: Every real symmetric matrix A can be written A = QΛQᵀ where Q is orthogonal and Λ is diagonal with real eigenvalues.
topics.intuition: The spectral theorem says symmetric matrices are 'pure stretching' in an orthonormal coordinate system — no rotation, no shearing. Just scaling along perpendicular axes.

steps.text: Find eigenvalues λ₁,…,λₙ of A (all real by symmetry).
Find corresponding eigenvectors; apply Gram-Schmidt within each eigenspace to get orthonormal eigenvectors.
Stack eigenvectors as columns of Q: Q is orthogonal.
A = QΛQᵀ (note Qᵀ not Q⁻¹ — they're equal for orthogonal Q).

matlab.note: for symmetric A, Q is orthogonal

mistakes: The spectral theorem applies to REAL SYMMETRIC matrices; for complex, it's Hermitian matrices
topics.example: PCA uses the spectral theorem on the covariance matrix to find uncorrelated directions of variance.

walkthrough.problem: Show that A's symmetry already guarantees what the spectral theorem promises: real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, i.e. A = QDQᵗ.

steps.note: A is symmetric, so the spectral theorem applies: A is guaranteed to have real eigenvalues.
Those real eigenvalues are exactly the ones already found.
The theorem also guarantees an orthonormal eigenbasis — exactly the Q built by normalizing the eigenvectors.
So the spectral decomposition A = QDQᵗ is exactly the orthogonal diagonalization already assembled.

topics.title: Orthogonal Diagonalization
topics.summary: A symmetric matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable: A = PDP⁻¹ = PDPᵀ where P is orthogonal.
topics.intuition: Ordinary diagonalization uses any eigenvector basis. Orthogonal diagonalization uses an ORTHONORMAL eigenvector basis — this is always possible for symmetric matrices and gives Pᵀ = P⁻¹.

steps.text: Find eigenvalues. For each, find the eigenspace (null space of A−λI).
Within each eigenspace, apply Gram-Schmidt if the eigenspace has dimension > 1.
Collect all orthonormal eigenvectors into P. Form D = diag(eigenvalues).
Verify: PᵀP = I (orthogonal) and A = PDPᵀ.

python.note: eigh gives orthonormal P for symmetric A

matlab.note: for symmetric A, P is automatically orthogonal

mistakes: If an eigenvalue has multiplicity > 1, apply Gram-Schmidt to its eigenspace before assembling P
topics.example: Stress analysis: principal stresses and axes from the (symmetric) stress tensor via orthogonal diagonalization.

walkthrough.problem: Because A is symmetric, replace P⁻¹ with Qᵗ — no matrix inversion needed — to orthogonally diagonalize A.

steps.note: Take the orthonormal Q built above, with the same D from Diagonalization.
AQ = QD as before, but now Q⁻¹ = Qᵗ, so multiply both sides by Qᵗ instead of inverting.

topics.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
topics.summary: Every matrix A = UΣVᵀ where U,V are orthogonal and Σ is diagonal with non-negative singular values.
topics.intuition: SVD is the most general decomposition — it works for ANY matrix (not just square or symmetric). It reveals the 'true geometry' of a linear transformation: rotate, scale along axes, rotate again.

steps.text: Singular values σᵢ = √(eigenvalues of AᵀA). Always real, non-negative.
V: orthonormal eigenvectors of AᵀA (right singular vectors).
U: orthonormal eigenvectors of AAᵀ (left singular vectors). Or compute uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ.
Rank = number of non-zero singular values. Condition number = σ_max/σ_min.

python.note: s = singular values (not a diagonal matrix)

matlab.note: S is the diagonal Σ matrix (not just values)

mistakes: NumPy returns s as a vector; MATLAB returns S as a matrix — know which you have before using
topics.example: Image compression: keep only the k largest singular values to get a rank-k approximation.

walkthrough.problem: Compute the SVD A = UΣVᵗ of A = [[1,1],[1,0],[0,1]], the same matrix used in QR/Gram-Schmidt, and connect the singular values to the eigenvalues of AᵗA.

steps.note: Form AᵗA (a real matrix multiplication, transpose included) — it's symmetric, so it's orthogonally diagonalizable.
Eigenvalues of AᵗA solve det(AᵗA−λI)=0 — the same characteristic-polynomial method as Eigenvalues.
Singular values are the square roots of these eigenvalues.
Right singular vectors v₁, v₂: solve (AᵗA−λI)v=0 for each eigenvalue, exactly as in Eigenvectors, then normalize.
Left singular vectors u_i = A v_i / σ_i.
Assemble the thin SVD A = UΣVᵗ (3×2 U, 2×2 Σ, 2×2 V) and verify it reproduces A.

topics.title: Least Squares
topics.summary: When Ax=b has no solution, find x̂ minimizing ‖b−Ax‖². The solution satisfies the normal equations AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb.
topics.intuition: Least squares finds the closest solution when exact solution doesn't exist — the projection of b onto the column space of A.

steps.text: b is inconsistent: it's not in col(A). Project b onto col(A).
Normal equations: AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb.
If A has full column rank, x̂ = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb (pseudoinverse).
More stable: use QR decomposition to solve R x̂ = Qᵀb.

matlab.note: MATLAB \ does least squares automatically when A is not square

mistakes: Normal equations (AᵀA)x = Aᵀb are mathematically correct but numerically unstable — prefer QR or lstsq
topics.example: Linear regression: fit a line y = a + bx to data points using least squares.

walkthrough.problem: Solve Ax≈b for A = [[1,1],[1,0],[0,1]] and b = (1,1,1), where b is genuinely not in the column space of A, via the normal equations and via the QR factorization from qr-decomposition — and check both methods agree.

steps.note: Check b is not in col(A): rank(A) = 2 but rank([A|b]) = 3, so Ax=b has no exact solution.
Method 1 — normal equations AᵗA x̂ = Aᵗb.
Method 2 — use Q, R from qr-decomposition (same A). First compute Qᵗb as two explicit dot products (rows of Qᵗ against b).
Now back-substitute into R x̂ = Qᵗb (R is upper triangular, so solve bottom-up). Row 2 first: √1.5 x̂₂ = 2/√6, and √1.5 = √6/2.
Row 1: √2 x̂₁ + (1/√2)x̂₂ = √2. Substitute x̂₂ = 2/3 and solve for x̂₁.
Both rows solved — Method 2 lands on exactly the same answer as the normal equations.
Numerically verified with numpy.linalg.lstsq(A, b) — returns the same x̂.

topics.title: Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse
topics.summary: A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ gives the best possible 'inverse' for any matrix — exact when A is invertible.
topics.intuition: The pseudoinverse solves Ax=b as well as possible: if it's consistent it gives the exact solution; if not, it gives the minimum-norm least-squares solution.

steps.text: From SVD A = UΣVᵀ, form Σ⁺ by inverting non-zero singular values.
A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ
The least-squares solution x̂ = A⁺b.
If A is square and invertible: A⁺ = A⁻¹.

mistakes: pinv is slow for large matrices — for least squares, use lstsq or QR instead
topics.example: Robotics: pseudoinverse of the Jacobian maps desired end-effector motion to joint velocities.

walkthrough.problem: Compute the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse A⁺ of A = [[1,1],[1,0],[0,1]] using the full-column-rank left-inverse formula, and confirm A⁺b reproduces the least-squares answer for b=(1,1,1).

steps.note: A has full column rank (rank 2), so the pseudoinverse is the left inverse A⁺ = (AᵗA)⁻¹Aᵗ.
AᵗA and its inverse (computed in least-squares).
Multiply by Aᵗ to get A⁺.
Apply A⁺ to b = (1,1,1) — matches the least-squares solution x̂ = (2/3, 2/3) exactly.
Verified numerically: numpy.linalg.pinv(A) gives the same matrix, and matches (AᵗA)⁻¹Aᵗ to machine precision.

topics.title: Linear Transformations
topics.summary: A function T: ℝⁿ→ℝᵐ is linear if T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) and T(cv)=cT(v).
topics.intuition: Linear transformations preserve the grid lines of vector space — lines stay straight, origin stays fixed. Every linear transformation has a matrix representation.

steps.text: Linearity conditions: additivity and homogeneity.
Matrix of T: columns are T(e₁), T(e₂), …, T(eₙ) — apply T to each basis vector.
Kernel = null space of A; Image = column space of A.
T is one-to-one iff kernel = {0}; onto iff image = ℝᵐ.

mistakes: Not every function from ℝⁿ to ℝᵐ is linear — check T(0) = 0 first
topics.example: Differentiation of polynomials is a linear transformation between polynomial spaces.

walkthrough.problem: Show that T(x) = Mx for M = [[2,1],[0,1]] is linear by computing T(v), and verifying T(v+w) = T(v)+T(w).

steps.note: Apply T to v by multiplying M times v.
Apply T to a second vector w the same way.
Add v and w first, then apply T to the sum.
Compare to T(v) + T(w) computed separately.
The two sides match, confirming additivity — but linearity needs BOTH additivity and scalar homogeneity. Check the second half: T(cv) = cT(v) for, say, c=3.
Scale v by c=3 first, then apply T.
Compare to c·T(v), scaling the already-computed T(v) by the same c=3.
Both additivity AND homogeneity hold, so T is genuinely linear — not just 'looks proportional'.
steps.latex: T(v+w)=T(v)+T(w) \ \text{ and } \ T(cv)=cT(v) \;\Longrightarrow\; T \text{ is linear}

topics.title: Change of Basis
topics.summary: Convert coordinates between different bases using the change-of-basis matrix P.
topics.intuition: A vector doesn't change — only its coordinates change when you switch bases. The change-of-basis matrix converts between these coordinate representations.

steps.text: If B = {b₁,…,bₙ} is a basis, build matrix P with bᵢ as columns.
Standard → B coordinates: [x]_B = P⁻¹x.
B → standard coordinates: x = P[x]_B.
Matrix A in basis B: [A]_B = P⁻¹AP (similar matrices represent same transformation).

mistakes: The change-of-basis matrix P goes from B-coordinates TO standard, not the other way
topics.example: Eigenvector basis: in the eigenvector basis, a diagonalizable matrix acts as pure scaling.

walkthrough.problem: Find the coordinates of v = (4,2) relative to the basis B = {(1,1), (1,−1)} of ℝ².

steps.note: Build the change-of-basis matrix P with the basis vectors as columns.
Set up a(1,1) + b(1,−1) = (4,2) as the linear system Pc = v.
Compute P⁻¹ for a 2×2 matrix: swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal, divide by det(P).
The coordinates of v in basis B are [v]_B = P⁻¹v.
Verify: plug a=3, b=1 back into the original combination.

topics.title: Positive Definite Matrices
topics.summary: A symmetric matrix S is positive definite if xᵀSx > 0 for all x ≠ 0, equivalently all eigenvalues > 0.
topics.intuition: Positive definite matrices are 'energy functions' — they always give a positive result when you plug in any non-zero vector. They have a unique Cholesky factorization and a unique minimum.

steps.text: Test 1: all eigenvalues > 0.
Test 2: all leading principal minors > 0 (Sylvester's criterion).
Test 3: S = AᵀA for some matrix A with independent columns.
Cholesky: if S is PD, then S = LLᵀ where L is lower triangular with positive diagonal.

matlab.line: try L = chol(S, 'lower'); disp('PD'); catch; disp('not PD'); end

mistakes: Semi-definite (xᵀSx ≥ 0) allows zero eigenvalues — not positive definite
topics.example: Covariance matrices are always positive semi-definite (and positive definite if non-degenerate).

walkthrough.problem: Show S is positive definite by checking its eigenvalues are positive and testing xᵗSx > 0 at x = (1,1).

steps.note: S is symmetric, so its eigenvalues are real — find them from the characteristic polynomial.
Factor and solve.
Both eigenvalues are positive, which is the eigenvalue test for positive definiteness.
Confirm directly with the quadratic-form test at a specific vector x = (1,1).

topics.title: Cholesky Decomposition
topics.summary: For symmetric positive definite S: S = LLᵀ where L is lower triangular with positive diagonal.
topics.intuition: Cholesky is the 'square root' of a positive definite matrix. Twice as fast as LU for symmetric matrices and guaranteed to be stable.

steps.text: Only works on symmetric positive definite matrices.
Compute L column by column using the Cholesky algorithm.
Half the work of LU because symmetry is exploited.
If cholesky fails (matrix not PD), you know the matrix is singular or indefinite.

mistakes: NumPy's cholesky returns lower triangular L where S = L @ L.T, not L.T @ L
topics.example: Monte Carlo simulation: Cholesky of the covariance matrix generates correlated random samples.

walkthrough.problem: Compute the Cholesky factor L of S, with S = LLᵗ and L lower triangular with positive diagonal.

steps.note: S is symmetric positive definite (eigenvalues 1, 3 > 0), so a Cholesky factorization exists.
Match the (1,1) entry: ℓ₁₁² = s₁₁.
Match the (2,1) entry: ℓ₁₁ℓ₂₁ = s₂₁.
Match the (2,2) entry: ℓ₂₁² + ℓ₂₂² = s₂₂.
Assemble L and verify LLᵗ recovers S exactly.

topics.title: Vector Spaces & Subspaces
topics.summary: A vector space satisfies 8 axioms. A subspace is a subset closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
topics.intuition: Any set where you can add elements and scale them — and the results stay in the set — is a vector space. Subspaces are 'smaller' vector spaces living inside larger ones.

steps.text: Subspace test: (1) contains 0, (2) closed under addition, (3) closed under scalar mult.
Key subspaces of A: null space, column space, row space, left null space.
Span of a set S = smallest subspace containing S.

python.line: # Check if [1,2,3] is in the span of {[1,0,1], [0,1,1]}

mistakes: A subspace must contain the zero vector — planes not through the origin are NOT subspaces
topics.example: All 2×2 symmetric matrices form a 3-dimensional vector space (dimension = 3).

walkthrough.problem: Using v = (3,−1,2) and w = (1,4,−1), confirm ℝ³ is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

steps.note: Closure under addition: v + w must still land in ℝ³.
Closure under scalar multiplication: scaling v by any c ∈ ℝ (here c=5) must still land in ℝ³.
Both results are ordinary vectors in ℝ³ — no operation produced anything outside the space, exactly what closure requires.
steps.latex: v+w \in \mathbb{R}^3 \ \text{ and } \ 5v \in \mathbb{R}^3 \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathbb{R}^3 \text{ is closed under } + \text{ and scalar mult.}

topics.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces
topics.summary: Every m×n matrix A has four associated subspaces: col(A), null(A), row(A), left null(A).
topics.intuition: These four subspaces come in two orthogonal pairs. Understanding them reveals the complete geometry of a linear system.

steps.text: Column space col(A) ⊆ ℝᵐ, dim = r.
Null space null(A) ⊆ ℝⁿ, dim = n−r.
Row space row(A) = col(Aᵀ) ⊆ ℝⁿ, dim = r.
Left null space null(Aᵀ) ⊆ ℝᵐ, dim = m−r.
Orthogonality: col(A) ⊥ null(Aᵀ) and row(A) ⊥ null(A).

mistakes: Row space and column space have the same dimension (rank), but live in different spaces
topics.example: Network flows: null space = circulations, left null space = cuts. The four subspaces reveal flow structure.

walkthrough.problem: Find all four fundamental subspaces of A and verify the rank-nullity relationships across all of them.

steps.note: Column space Col(A) ⊆ ℝ³: span of the pivot columns of A. dim = rank(A) = r = 2.
Null space Null(A) ⊆ ℝ³: solutions of Ax = 0. dim = n − r = 3 − 2 = 1.
Row space Row(A) = Col(Aᵗ) ⊆ ℝ³: span of the pivot ROWS of A (rows 1 and 3, since RREF shows row 2 became all-zero — it was 2× row 1). dim = r = 2.
Left null space Null(Aᵗ) ⊆ ℝ³: solve Aᵗy = 0. dim = m − r = 3 − 2 = 1.
Check both rank-nullity relationships: one in ℝⁿ (domain side), one in ℝᵘ (codomain side). Here m = n = 3.

topics.title: Markov Chains
topics.summary: A Markov chain is a process where the state at step k+1 depends only on step k. The steady state is an eigenvector.
topics.intuition: Multiply the state vector by the transition matrix each step. Eventually it converges to the steady-state distribution — the eigenvector for eigenvalue 1.

steps.text: Transition matrix A: Aᵢⱼ = probability of going from state j to state i.
Columns sum to 1 (stochastic matrix); eigenvalue 1 always exists.
State at step k: xₖ = Aᵏx₀. As k→∞, xₖ → steady state.
Steady state: find null space of (A−I) — same as eigenvector for λ=1.

mistakes: Columns must sum to 1, not rows — this is the column stochastic convention
topics.example: Google PageRank: web pages as states, hyperlinks as transitions, steady state = page importance.

walkthrough.problem: Find the steady-state distribution of the Markov chain with transition matrix P = [[0.7, 0.4], [0.3, 0.6]] by finding the eigenvector for eigenvalue 1.

steps.note: Confirm columns sum to 1 (stochastic matrix), which guarantees λ=1 is an eigenvalue.
Verify λ=1 by checking det(P−I)=0.
The other eigenvalue, from the trace: tr(P) = λ₁+λ₂ = 1.3, so λ₂ = 0.3.
Solve (P−I)v = 0 for the eigenvector of λ=1.
Normalize so the entries sum to 1 — this is the steady-state probability distribution.
Verified with numpy.linalg.eig(P): eigenvalues (1, 0.3), and P·π = π to machine precision.

topics.title: Quadratic Forms
topics.summary: A quadratic form Q(x) = xᵀAx for symmetric A. Its sign (positive/negative/indefinite) is determined by eigenvalues.
topics.intuition: A quadratic form is a multi-variable generalization of ax² — it's a 'bowl' in n-D space. Positive definite = bowl opening up, negative definite = bowl opening down, indefinite = saddle.

steps.text: Write Q(x) = xᵀAx where A is the associated symmetric matrix.
Diagonalize A = QΛQᵀ, change variables y = Qᵀx.
Q(x) = Σ λᵢyᵢ² (sum of squares — the 'principal axes form').
Sign of Q depends on signs of eigenvalues.

python.line: def Q(x): return x @ A @ x

mistakes: The matrix A of a quadratic form must be symmetric — if it's not, symmetrize it first: A = (A+Aᵀ)/2
topics.example: Inertia tensor: Q(ω) = ωᵀIω is the rotational kinetic energy (quadratic form).

walkthrough.problem: Expand the quadratic form Q(x) = xᵗSx explicitly and evaluate it at x = (1,1).

steps.note: Multiply out xᵗSx symbolically, term by term.
Finish the dot product to get the explicit quadratic form.
Evaluate at x = (1,1) — matches the xᵗSx = 6 computed directly in Positive Definite.
Since S has eigenvalues 1, 3 (both positive), the spectral theorem's principal-axes form Q = λ₁y₁²+λ₂y₂² is a sum of positive terms, confirming Q(x) > 0 for all x ≠ 0.

topics.title: Diagonalizability Test
topics.summary: A matrix is diagonalizable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors iff geometric multiplicity = algebraic multiplicity for every eigenvalue.
topics.intuition: A repeated eigenvalue might cause problems if the eigenspace is 'too small' (defective). The test: enough independent eigenvectors?

steps.text: Find all eigenvalues and their algebraic multiplicities (root multiplicities of char. poly.).
For each eigenvalue, find dim of null(A−λI) = geometric multiplicity.
A is diagonalizable iff geom. mult. = alg. mult. for every eigenvalue.
Sufficient condition: n distinct eigenvalues guarantees diagonalizability.

python.note: also λ=5 repeated, but IS diagonalizable (it's 5I)

matlab.note: MATLAB still returns something, but V is not well-conditioned

mistakes: All distinct eigenvalues → diagonalizable; repeated eigenvalues → CHECK geometric multiplicity
topics.example: The identity matrix I has λ=1 with multiplicity n but IS diagonalizable (it already is diagonal).

walkthrough.problem: Confirm A is diagonalizable by checking algebraic multiplicity = geometric multiplicity for every eigenvalue.

steps.note: Each eigenvalue is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial λ(λ−4)(λ−2)=0, so algebraic multiplicity is 1 for each.
Each eigenspace found earlier is a span of a single vector, so geometric multiplicity is also 1.
Geometric multiplicity = algebraic multiplicity for every eigenvalue, so the three eigenvectors are automatically linearly independent.
Three independent eigenvectors in ℝ³ means A is diagonalizable.

topics.title: Matrix Similarity
topics.summary: A and B are similar if B = P⁻¹AP for some invertible P. Similar matrices represent the same linear transformation in different bases.
topics.intuition: Similarity is a change of basis. If you change the coordinates you use, the same transformation looks like a different matrix — but it IS the same transformation.

steps.text: Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues, determinant, trace, and rank.
B = P⁻¹AP means B is A in the P-basis.
Diagonalization is a special case: D = P⁻¹AP where D is diagonal.

mistakes: Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues but not the same eigenvectors
topics.example: A rotation matrix and its diagonal form are similar — same rotation, described in different coordinate systems.

walkthrough.problem: Show A and D = diag(0,4,2) are similar via A = PDP⁻¹, using the same P from Diagonalization.

steps.note: Two matrices B and A are similar if B = S⁻¹AS for some invertible S — they represent the same linear map in different bases.
steps.latex: B \sim A \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \exists\, S\ \text{invertible such that}\ B = S^{-1}AS

steps.note: From Diagonalization, A = PDP⁻¹. Solve for D to see P playing the role of S.
This is exactly the similarity relation with S = P: D is A viewed in the eigenvector basis. P⁻¹ was computed explicitly in Diagonalization — reuse it rather than leaving it symbolic.
Similar matrices share eigenvalues, trace, and determinant — check trace as a quick sanity test.

topics.title: Matrix Exponential
topics.summary: eᴬ = Σ Aᵏ/k! solves differential equations ẋ = Ax: the solution is x(t) = eᴬᵗx₀.
topics.intuition: The matrix exponential is to ODEs what the scalar exponential is to scalar ODEs. Diagonalization makes it computable: eᴬ = PeᴰP⁻¹.

steps.text: For diagonal D: eᴰ = diag(eᵈ¹, eᵈ², …)
For diagonalizable A = PDP⁻¹: eᴬ = PeᴰP⁻¹
Solution to ẋ = Ax with x(0) = x₀: x(t) = eᴬᵗx₀

mistakes: expm(A) ≠ exp(A): exp gives element-wise exponential, expm gives the matrix exponential
topics.example: Quantum mechanics: time evolution operator e^{-iHt/ℏ} is a matrix exponential.

walkthrough.problem: Compute e^{At} using the diagonalization A = PDP⁻¹.

steps.note: For a diagonalizable matrix, the matrix exponential factors through D: only the diagonal needs exponentiating.
Exponentiate each eigenvalue on the diagonal of D, using λ ∈ {0, 4, 2} found earlier.
steps.latex: e^{Dt} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{0\cdot t} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & e^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & e^{2t} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & e^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & e^{2t} \end{bmatrix}

steps.note: Assemble the full solution structure — P and P⁻¹ sandwich the exponentiated diagonal. P⁻¹ was computed explicitly in Diagonalization, not just left as a symbol.
This solves ẋ = Ax: any solution is x(t) = e^{At}x_0, decaying/growing along each eigen-direction independently at rate λ.
steps.latex: x(t) = e^{At}x_0,\qquad \text{component along } v_0 \text{ stays constant } (e^{0\cdot t}=1),\ \text{component along } v_4 \text{ grows as } e^{4t}

topics.title: Span
topics.summary: The span of a set S is all possible linear combinations of vectors in S.
topics.intuition: Span is the 'reach' of a set of vectors. Two non-parallel vectors in ℝ³ span a plane; three non-coplanar vectors span all of ℝ³.

steps.text: span(v₁,…,vₖ) = {c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ : cᵢ ∈ ℝ}
Span is always a subspace.
A set of vectors spans ℝⁿ iff their matrix has rank n.

mistakes: Adding a vector that's in the current span doesn't increase the span
topics.example: The three RGB channels span the 3-D color space — any color is a combination of red, green, blue.

walkthrough.problem: Write w = (4,2) as a linear combination a·u₁ + b·u₂ of u₁ = (1,1) and u₂ = (1,−1).

steps.note: Set up a·u₁ + b·u₂ = w as a linear system in the unknowns a, b.
Add the two equations to eliminate b.
Substitute back to find b.
Verify the combination reproduces w.

topics.title: Coordinates & Dimension
topics.summary: Dimension of a subspace = size of any basis for it. Coordinates give unique representation in a chosen basis.
topics.intuition: Dimension counts degrees of freedom. ℝⁿ has dimension n. A plane through the origin has dimension 2, no matter what space it's embedded in.

steps.text: All bases for a subspace have the same number of vectors — that's the dimension.
Unique representation: given basis B and vector x, there is exactly one way to write x = c₁b₁+…+cₙbₙ.
Dimension formula: dim(col(A)) + dim(null(A)) = n (columns of A)

mistakes: Dimension is a property of the space, not of how it's described — different bases, same dimension
topics.example: 2-D images have a very high pixel dimension, but typically lie in a low-dimensional 'manifold'.

walkthrough.problem: Express the coordinates of v = (4,2) relative to basis B = {(1,1), (1,−1)} found above, and confirm they reconstruct v.

steps.note: From the change-of-basis computation, the coordinate vector relative to B is:
This means v is uniquely written as a combination of b₁ and b₂ with these two scalars.
Substitute the actual basis vectors and expand component-by-component.
This matches v exactly, confirming the coordinates are correct — and they're unique because B is a basis.

topics.title: Trace
topics.summary: tr(A) = sum of diagonal entries = sum of eigenvalues.
topics.intuition: Trace is a simple but powerful invariant. It tells you the sum of eigenvalues without computing any of them.

steps.text: tr(A) = A₁₁ + A₂₂ + … + Aₙₙ
tr(A) = λ₁ + λ₂ + … + λₙ (sum of eigenvalues)
tr(AB) = tr(BA); tr(A+B) = tr(A)+tr(B)

mistakes: tr(AB) = tr(BA) but tr(ABC) ≠ tr(BAC) in general — only cyclic permutations are equal
topics.example: In quantum mechanics, the trace of the density matrix = 1 (total probability = 1).

walkthrough.problem: Show that tr(A) equals the sum of the eigenvalues found in the Eigenvalues walkthrough.

steps.note: Trace is the sum of the diagonal entries.
Simplify.
The Eigenvalues walkthrough found λ(A) = {0, 4, 2} for this exact matrix. Sum them.
The two sums match, confirming tr(A) = Σλᵢ.

topics.title: Norms & Condition Number
topics.summary: Matrix norms measure the 'size' of a matrix. The condition number κ = ‖A‖·‖A⁻¹‖ measures numerical sensitivity.
topics.intuition: A large condition number means the system is ill-conditioned — small changes in b lead to large changes in the solution x. SVD reveals the condition number directly.

steps.text: Vector norms: ‖v‖₂ (Euclidean), ‖v‖₁ (sum of abs), ‖v‖_∞ (max abs)
Induced 2-norm of A = σ_max (largest singular value)
Frobenius norm: ‖A‖_F = √(Σ Aᵢⱼ²) = √(Σ σᵢ²)
Condition number: κ₂(A) = σ_max/σ_min. If κ >> 1, beware numerical errors.

mistakes: High condition number doesn't mean the matrix is singular — it just means small errors amplify greatly
topics.example: Hilbert matrix: condition number grows exponentially with size — a classic ill-conditioned system.

walkthrough.problem: Compute the spectral norm ‖A‖₂ and the Frobenius norm ‖A‖_F of A = [[1,1],[1,0],[0,1]].

steps.note: Spectral (operator) 2-norm = largest singular value, found via SVD.
Frobenius norm: square root of the sum of squares of all entries.
Cross-check: Frobenius norm also equals the square root of the sum of squares of the singular values.

topics.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
topics.summary: PCA finds the directions of maximum variance in data using the spectral theorem on the covariance matrix.
topics.intuition: PCA rotates your coordinate system so the first axis points in the direction of greatest spread, the second in the next greatest (and perpendicular), etc. It's the spectral theorem applied to data.

steps.text: Center the data: subtract the mean from each sample.
Compute the covariance matrix C = (1/n)XᵀX.
Eigendecompose C = QΛQᵀ — columns of Q are principal components.
Equivalently: SVD of the data matrix X = UΣVᵀ; V contains principal components.

mistakes: Always center data before PCA — without centering, the first PC just points at the mean
topics.example: Face recognition: PCA on face images gives 'eigenfaces' — the main modes of facial variation.

walkthrough.problem: Run PCA on the 4 points (5,3), (3,5), (-1,1), (1,-1): center the data, form the covariance matrix, and find its eigenvalues/eigenvectors to identify the principal components.

steps.note: Compute the mean: average each coordinate across all 4 points.
Center the data by subtracting the mean from every point.

Form Xcᵗ Xc entry by entry — this is an ordinary matrix multiplication, same mechanics as Matrix Operations: entry (1,1) is the dot product of column 1 with itself, entry (1,2) is column 1 dotted with column 2.
Assemble Xcᵗ Xc and divide by n=4 to get the covariance matrix C.
Eigendecompose C (symmetric, so orthogonally diagonalizable) — same characteristic-polynomial method as Eigenvalues.
Eigenvectors: solve (C−λI)v=0 for each λ, exactly as in Eigenvectors. λ=8 gives the direction of maximum variance (the first principal component); λ=2 is orthogonal to it.
Verified with numpy.linalg.eigh(C) — eigenvalues (2, 8) and matching eigenvectors to machine precision.
